title: The young colt
hookLine: Bhaddali won't keep the one-meal rule; a good horse is trained step by step

cards: The Buddha tells the monks he eats once a day, at one sitting, and feels light and healthy for it. He invites them to do the same. One monk, Bhaddāli, says flatly: I can't.
I'd worry about it. The Buddha offers a compromise: eat part at the meal, and take the rest to eat later. Bhaddāli says no to that too.
And then, for the entire three months of the rains retreat, he avoids the Buddha completely. A very human pair: the rule he won't keep, and the teacher he stops looking in the eye.

teach.b: At the end of the retreat, the monks are sewing a robe for the Buddha before he sets out on his travels, and they tell Bhaddāli: this is your chance. Go and make it right. So he does.
He admits he was foolish and wrong. The Buddha accepts it, but doesn't rush past it either.
He tells Bhaddāli plainly what he'd failed to see: people had noticed, monks and nuns and lay followers, that he wasn't fulfilling the training.

Later Bhaddāli asks a fair question: why are some monks pressed hard over a fault and others left alone? It depends, the Buddha says, on whether they keep making excuses, or whether they can hear correction.
Then he recalls a picture. A skilled horse trainer gets a fine young colt. What does he do first?
He gets it used to wearing the bit.
And the colt fights it. It twists and resists, because it's never done anything like this before. But with repetition, step by step, it settles.
Then the trainer adds the harness.

teach.h: THEN THE HARNESS, ONE STAGE AT A TIME.
teach.b: Then keeping in step, running in a circle, galloping, one stage at a time, until the colt is worthy of a king.
That's the training. Not one leap: a long series of small things, each strange at first.
The colt isn't a bad horse for resisting the bit. Resisting is what a colt does on its first day. Repetition, stage by stage, is what settles it.

how: Theravada monks and nuns do not eat after midday, and some keep to one meal a day; communities correct members who struggle with a rule; lay Buddhists who keep eight precepts on observance days also skip the evening meal.

o: training, learned one stage at a time
a punishment for breaking a rule

games.q: Bhaddāli and the colt: tap the pairs.
p: three months he avoided the Buddha
adds one stage at a time

s: the colt resisting the bit marks it as a bad horse
resisting is what a colt does at first; with repetition it settles.
Bhaddāli came to apologize while the monks were sewing a robe for the Buddha
they told him this was his chance before the Buddha set out on his travels.
the Buddha forced the monks to eat once a day from that day on
in this sutta he invites it and even offers Bhaddāli a compromise.

games.q: you're Bhaddāli. for three months you've avoided your teacher over a rule you wouldn't keep. the monks say: go now. what does the text say happens?
o: he goes, admits his fault, and is heard
the Buddha refuses to see him
games.why: he admits he was wrong, and the Buddha accepts it, while also telling him clearly what he'd failed to see.

practice: Think of one small discipline you've been resisting, a bedtime, a budget, a daily walk, something someone wise suggested, and notice the twist in you that says I can't.
You don't have to argue with it: picture the colt with the bit, resisting, and then, a little later, quieter. Choose just the bit, one small piece, not the whole harness, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Sikkha. Training: a good horse learns step by step, and resists at first, because everything new feels wrong.

orig.note: Pali sikkhā: training. the whole path is called a training, step by step.

carryVoice: Your line: the colt learns. One strange step at a time, and then the next. See you tomorrow.
